scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I should apologize to my mom after our conversation about the wedding dress. Let me start by understanding the situation. I'm getting married, and I've decided on a small, semi-formal beach wedding. My mom suggested going to a bridal shop in town, but I told her I don't want a white dress because that's all they have. I think the whole white dress thing is outdated, starting with Queen Victoria, so it's not an ancient tradition. Plus, the symbolism of white meaning purity or innocence doesn't resonate with me, especially since I'm not exactly "innocent." My mom asked why I didn't want a white dress, and I gave her a few reasons. First, the historical context, which she didn't find sufficient. Then, I mentioned my lack of innocence, which was a tough conversation. She pushed further, and eventually, I told her that her being the only one in the family to wear white and end up divorced made me not confident in white dresses. She got really quiet and started crying, saying she tried her best and that my words were cruel because she was upset about the divorce. I haven't apologized yet. I feel like she backed me into a corner by not accepting my initial reasons and made me justify myself, which I shouldn't have to do because it's my wedding. I think if she had accepted my choice earlier, we wouldn't be in this situation. Now, I'm wondering if I should apologize. On one hand, I stood my ground because it's my wedding, and I have the right to choose my dress. On the other hand, I hurt her feelings, and she was vulnerable because of the divorce. Maybe I should have handled it more gently, especially since she was emotional. I also need to consider our relationship. We've had some tough times, and I don't want this to cause a bigger issue. Apologizing might help mend things, but I also don't want to backtrack on my decision. Maybe I can apologize for the way I expressed myself without changing my choice. I should also think about how my mom felt. She was trying to support me, but I made her feel like her efforts weren't enough. That must have been really hard for her, especially since the divorce was a sensitive topic. I might have crossed a line by bringing up the divorce in that context. In the end, I think the best approach is to apologize for how I made her feel, acknowledge her feelings, and reaffirm that her support means a lot to me. I can explain that my choice is about me and my wedding, not about her, and that I appreciate her understanding.
